name: Padimate O

lead: Padimate O is an oily PABA-derived UVB filter that was common in sunscreens and lip products to prevent sunburn and sun-driven skin aging.

It absorbs UVB light. Researchers have debated its photochemistry: in vitro work suggested indirect DNA damage on irradiation, while hairless-mouse studies reported no carcinogenic effect. It is approved by the US FDA among other agencies, and appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.

paras: It was used as one filter in SPF creams and lip balms. It is less common now and mostly appears in ingredient-history discussions.
Yeast and cell studies raised photomutagenicity and hormone-receptor questions, while hairless-mouse studies found no carcinogenicity. Labels advise stopping use if rash occurs.

angle.text: Padimate O is an older PABA-derived UVB filter once common in sunscreens and lip products. By absorbing UVB it cuts sunburn and the sun damage behind premature skin aging. It is rarely used now, and appearance outcomes were not studied for it specifically.

lead: Padimate O (octyl dimethyl PABA, 2-ethylhexyl 4-dimethylaminobenzoate, sold as Escalol 507) is an oily, water-insoluble ester related to PABA that has been used as a UVB filter in sunscreens and lip products [1]. It is approved by one or more agencies including the US FDA, per Wikipedia [1].
Researchers have debated its photochemistry: in vitro work suggested indirect DNA damage on irradiation, while hairless-mouse studies reported no carcinogenic effect [1].

paras: It is used in some sunscreens and lip products; a US label lists padimate O with oxybenzone in a lip product to prevent sunburn and protect against windburn and cracked lips [2].

A 1993 yeast study reported sunlight-induced mutagenicity, and its photobiology resembles Michler's ketone, which is photocarcinogenic in rodents; however, several hairless-mouse studies found no carcinogenicity and reported reduced UV-induced tumours [1]. Cell assays found estrogenic activity for some UV screens [3] and antiandrogenic activity for several UV filters [4]. Sunscreen allergy series have included UV filters in photoallergy testing [5][6]. Skin penetration and keratinocyte toxicity of sunscreens have also been studied [7].
UV filters including those like it have been detected in beach waters [8] and are covered in a systematic ecological risk review [9].

No clinical trials of padimate O itself for appearance outcomes were found. Registered SPF-testing studies of sunscreen products have been run by manufacturers [10][11], and a Phase 1 study examined a nanoparticle sunblock [12]; these are not specific to padimate O.
